surveillance.principle: Scout never auto-publishes a clinical change. Machines WATCH; humans DECIDE. An automated pipeline that silently rewrote a drug dose would be the single most dangerous thing this product could do.

tiers.what: Poll public feeds for changes affecting entries in the library

sources.name: PubMed E-utilities
sources.method: Saved searches per high-risk topic, esearch by date window

sources.name: ClinicalTrials.gov API v2
sources.method: Watch trials linked from trial entries for results posting

sources.name: National programme sites (NTBLCP, NMEP, FMoH)
sources.method: Scheduled page-hash diff; many have no feed, so hashing is the pragmatic answer

sources.name: NAFDAC alerts
sources.method: Page diff — substandard and falsified product alerts

sources.name: Journal tables of contents
sources.method: RSS for NEJM, Lancet, BMJ, JAMA, Lancet Global Health

tiers.output: A change candidate with: source, date, URL, diff snippet, and the entry IDs whose search terms it matches.

tiers.what: Rank candidates so reviewers see the dangerous ones first
score_inputs: Hazard level of the affected entries (critical entries jump the queue)
Whether it contradicts current text (keyword opposition detection)
How long since that entry was last reviewed
tiers.output: Prioritised review queue with a suggested reviewer.

tiers.what: A named clinical reviewer opens the candidate beside the current entry text and chooses: no change / minor edit / major revision / withdraw entry
tiers.gate: Nothing moves past here without a named human. The system has no path to skip this.

tiers.what: Approved change creates a NEW entry version
rules: Old version is retained and remains addressable — never overwritten
content_hash changes; approved_for_release resets and must be re-granted
Change note is written in plain language and shown on the entry
Users who used the old version in the last 90 days get a 'this has changed' flag
Offline packages get a delta, not a full re-download

user_facing_signals: Each entry shows: last checked date, next check due, and who signed it off.
An entry past its review date shows a soft 'due for review' marker and is ranked lower in search.
A superseded entry shows a banner linking to the current version.
Offline users see the date their package was built, so they know how stale they might be.

the_other_direction.name: User signal — the cheapest surveillance you have
inputs: Zero-result query log (3+ hits in a week promotes to backlog)
'This looks wrong' button on every entry, with a free-text box
Which checklist items get ticked and which get skipped — a consistently skipped item is usually an item that cannot be done here
Which entries get opened repeatedly in one shift — that is a workflow gap, not curiosity
the_other_direction.why: Your users know before your feeds do that the national protocol changed, because they were at the training. Give them one tap to tell you.

honest_limits: Feed watching catches published changes. It does not catch a state ministry circular, a verbal change at a training day, or a stockout that makes the recommended drug unavailable.
Page-hash diffing is noisy — expect false positives from cookie banners and rotating banners. Hash the main content region, not the whole page.
Do not build this in month one. Ship the library first with honest review dates. Surveillance matters when you have 500 entries and cannot remember what needs checking.

engagement.the_goal_restated: Not 'time in app'. A clinician who spends longer in your EHR is not a success — they are away from a patient. The goal is: they come BACK, they trust it, and they leave slightly better than they arrived.

what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.scout_form: CARD OF THE SHIFT — one flashcard from an entry relevant to the ward they are on, shown once per shift on the dashboard. Answer or skip. No penalty.

what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.apply: CAUTIOUSLY. A streak that punishes a doctor for a busy night shift is hostile. Use a forgiving streak: weekly, not daily; freezes automatically on days off.
what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.scout_form: 'You've checked something 4 weeks running.' No loss animation. No guilt.

what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.apply: Show whether they were right instantly, with the one-line why.
what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.scout_form: Flip the card, show the answer plus a link to the full entry.
'You've now seen 34 of the 51 emergency cards.' Progress against a real body of knowledge, not an invented currency.

what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.apply: Spaced repetition on missed cards only.
what_to_borrow_from_duolingo.scout_form: Missed cards return in 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 21 days. This is the single highest-value learning mechanic and it is cheap to build.

what_NOT_to_borrow: Leaderboards between clinicians. Competition around clinical knowledge creates concealment of uncertainty, which is exactly the opposite of what a safe department needs.
Loss animations, sad mascots, guilt mechanics. These are for a language app, not a hospital.
Streak-breaking punishment. Someone was on call.
Anything that gates clinical content behind a game. Emergency content is ALWAYS one tap away, always, for everyone, with no progress requirement.

curiosity_hooks.where: A collapsed line at the bottom of any calculator
curiosity_hooks.example: On the drip card: 'Why 60?' → 'Because you set the rate per MINUTE but the order is per HOUR, so you divide by 60.'
From the drip card → potassium correction, blood transfusion, child maintenance fluid
'The most-missed card on this ward this month: which weight for tidal volume.'
'DKA criteria updated — the anion gap is no longer part of the diagnosis. See what changed.'
'FEAST (2011) — why we stopped giving routine fluid boluses to African children.'

measure: Time to answer (target under 15 seconds from tap to the number)
Percentage of searches ending in an opened entry
Checklist completion rate on high-risk procedures
'This looks wrong' reports per 1000 opens (a rising number is good — it means trust)
do_not_optimise: Daily active users as a headline
